cards.back: **Identical** antibodies made from one cloned cell, each binding to one specific antigen.

cards.front: Why is specificity the main advantage of monoclonal antibodies?
cards.back: Identical antibodies bind the same **target**, so a test can identify a chosen molecule and a treatment can aim at cells carrying a chosen antigen.
cards.hint: Think about what a test or treatment needs to hit.

cards.front: What are the four main steps in producing monoclonal antibodies?
cards.back: 1) Collect lymphocytes from a mouse exposed to the antigen. 2) Fuse them with tumour cells to form **hybridoma cells**. 3) Select a hybridoma making the required antibody. 4) Clone and grow it, then collect and purify its antibodies.
cards.hint: Start with what the mouse is exposed to.

cards.front: Why is a hybridoma used instead of ordinary lymphocytes to make monoclonal antibodies?
cards.back: Normal lymphocytes make the antibody but do not grow indefinitely. The **hybridoma** combines antibody production with repeated division, giving a continuing supply of the same antibody.
cards.hint: Compare how a normal lymphocyte behaves over time with the fused cell.

cards.back: A test that checks a sample for a **sign of a condition**, such as a particular molecule.

cards.front: How does a monoclonal antibody pregnancy test produce a visible result?
cards.back: Antibodies in the test **bind hCG** in urine if it is present, and this binding helps produce a visible result.

cards.front: What does the control indicator in a pregnancy test show?
cards.back: Whether the test has **worked**, even when the result is negative.
cards.hint: Think about what a negative result could mean without it.

cards.front: Why is a negative pregnancy test result unreliable if the control indicator fails?
cards.back: The **test may not have worked**, so a negative result gives no valid evidence either way.
cards.hint: Consider what the control is checking.

cards.front: What does a fluorescent label show about a monoclonal antibody?
cards.back: It reveals **where binding occurred**, so the bound molecule or cell can be seen with suitable equipment. It does not change what the antibody binds.

cards.front: How does an antibody carrying a toxic drug treat a cancer?
cards.back: The antibody binds a **surface antigen** on the cancer cell, and the attached toxic drug is delivered there to damage or kill it.
cards.hint: Name the antigen, the binding, then the effect on the cell.

cards.front: Why does an antibody treatment only work on some cancers?
cards.back: It works only when the cancer cells carry the **antigen** that the antibody recognises.
cards.hint: Think about what the antibody needs in order to bind.

cards.front: Why can targeted cancer treatment still cause side effects?
cards.back: Specific binding does not mean only diseased cells are affected. **Healthy cells** may carry the same antigen, so they can also be harmed.
cards.hint: Think about where else the antigen might be found in the body.

cards.front: What are two limitations of monoclonal antibodies?
cards.back: Producing and testing an antibody for a target takes **time and resources**, and it may bind healthy cells, causing side effects or unwanted immune reactions.
